findings.title: Cache entries survive rejected device-limit writes
findings.body: The device is added to the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs. When the database returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the cache entry remains; the next request for that device returns at the cache check without consulting the store, so `Authenticate` succeeds and the configured limit is bypassed for requests handled by this process. Only cache the device after a successful store write, or remove the entry on error.

findings.title: Concurrent requests can exceed the configured limit
findings.body: The device count and insert/update are separate operations with no transaction or locking. If the active count is one below the limit, concurrent requests can both observe that count and insert different devices, exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the check and insert atomically (including across Grafana instances), for example with a transaction and appropriate locking.

findings.title: MySQL may report unchanged updates as limit failures
findings.body: When the limit is reached, an existing device is updated and success is inferred from `RowsAffected()`. MySQL commonly reports zero affected rows when an UPDATE matches a row but all assigned values are unchanged; timestamps may also be stored only to second precision. Such a request is incorrectly returned as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, rejecting a device that should remain allowed. Determine whether the row exists independently of changed-row count, or use a database setting/query strategy that reports matched rows.
